lessons.title: How the web works (browsers, servers, HTML)
objectives: Explain what happens between typing a URL and a page appearing on screen (DNS, request, response, render).
Describe the role of HTML as the structural language of every web page.
Open browser DevTools and inspect a live page's HTML.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Every website you have ever visited — including the three projects you will build this module — starts the same way: a browser asks a server for an HTML file, the server sends it back, and the browser reads it top to bottom to build the page. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is not a programming language in the loops-and-variables sense — it is a markup language: a set of tags that describe *what each piece of content is* (a heading, a paragraph, an image, a link), never how it looks. That separation — structure in HTML, appearance in CSS — is the single most important idea in this module, and it is exactly how `index.html` and `styles.css` are split in every project you will open below.
lessons.homework: Open DevTools on three websites you use daily and inspect their HTML. For each, name one semantic tag you spot (e.g. `<nav>`, `<header>`, `<article>`) and what content it wraps. Then skim the "Personal Landing Page" starter `index.html` you'll build on in Lesson 2.
lessons.checkpoint: Follow along with the concept walkthrough

lessons.title: HTML structure and semantic elements
objectives: Write a valid HTML5 document with the correct boilerplate (doctype, head, body).
Use semantic elements (header, nav, main, section, footer) instead of generic divs where they communicate meaning.
Structure a real one-page site into logical sections.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Semantic HTML means choosing tags for what content *is*, not how it happens to look — a `<nav>` for navigation, a `<section>` for a themed block of content, a `<footer>` for closing info. Browsers, screen readers, and search engines all use these tags to understand your page, which is why "everything is a `<div>`" is a beginner habit worth breaking early.

lessons.title: CSS basics: colors, fonts, spacing
objectives: Apply CSS using an external stylesheet linked from HTML.
Use selectors, the box model (margin/border/padding), colors, and web fonts confidently.
Finish a fully styled, single-page site from a bare HTML structure.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) answers the question HTML deliberately leaves open: how should this look? Every visual property — color, spacing, typography — is set through a selector (which elements) plus a declaration block (which properties). "Cascading" means rules can override each other by specificity and source order, which is why organized, external stylesheets (like `styles.css` here) beat inline styles almost every time.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Flexbox solves one-dimensional layout — arranging items in a row or a column so they distribute space, align, and reorder without manual pixel math. `justify-content` controls spacing along the main axis, `align-items` controls the cross axis. This is the layout tool behind the portfolio's nav bar and project card row you will build today.

lessons.title: Responsive design and mobile-first
objectives: Write CSS mobile-first, then layer on `min-width` media queries for larger screens.
Use relative units (%, rem, vw) instead of fixed pixels where it matters.
Test a real layout at phone, tablet, and desktop widths.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Mobile-first means writing your default (no-media-query) CSS for the smallest screen, then adding `@media (min-width: ...)` rules to enhance the layout as space allows — the opposite of designing desktop-first and cramming it down later. You will lay the responsive foundation for the Product Showcase Site with this approach today.

lessons.title: Animations and hover effects
objectives: Use CSS `transition` for smooth property changes on hover/focus.
Write a basic `@keyframes` animation.
Apply restrained, purposeful motion that improves usability rather than distracting from it.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

A `transition` smoothly interpolates a CSS property change (e.g. `transform`, `opacity`) over time instead of snapping instantly — that's what makes a hover effect feel polished instead of janky. `@keyframes` goes further, defining a full animation sequence. You will finish the Product Showcase Site today with real hover/transition polish.

lessons.title: JavaScript fundamentals (variables, functions, loops)
objectives: Declare variables correctly with `let`/`const` and explain why `var` is avoided.
Write and call functions, including arrow functions.
Use `for`/`for...of` loops and array methods (`map`, `filter`) on real data.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

JavaScript is the only language that runs natively in every browser, which is why it is the language of web interactivity. Today is a fast, practical refresher on the building blocks — variables, functions, loops — aimed specifically at what you need for this module's three apps: reading and changing data, and reacting to what the user does.
lessons.homework: In your browser's Console, write and run: a variable declared with `let`/`const`, a small function that takes a parameter and returns a value, and one `.map()` or `for...of` loop over an array of at least 4 items. Save all three snippets — you'll reuse these exact patterns in the Interactive To-Do App next lesson.

The DOM (Document Object Model) is the live, in-memory tree of every element on the page — JavaScript reads and rewrites it to change what the user sees, without reloading the page. lessons.title: Why React exists and how components work
objectives: Explain the problem React solves versus manually updating the DOM.
Describe a component as a function that returns UI.
Set up a React project with Vite and run it locally.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

As apps grow, manually finding and updating DOM elements (Module 2's approach) gets unmanageable — React instead lets you describe UI as a function of state ("given this data, render this") and handles the DOM updates for you. A component is just a JavaScript function that returns markup; this module's three projects are built entirely out of small, composed components.
lessons.homework: Create a new React project with Vite (`npm create vite@latest`) and get it running locally. Write your own component that takes a `name` prop and returns a greeting, then render it twice in `App.jsx` with different names — the same reusable-component pattern the E-commerce Product Page uses for product cards.

lessons.title: JSX, props, and component trees
objectives: Write JSX that mixes markup and JavaScript expressions.
Pass data into a component via props and render it.
Break a page into a tree of reusable components.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

JSX looks like HTML but compiles to real JavaScript function calls — it is not a template language, which is why `{expression}` syntax works anywhere inside it. Props are how a parent component passes data down to a child, read-only, the same way a function receives arguments. You will structure the e-commerce product page as a tree of components today.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Props flow data down; `useState` gives a component its own local memory that persists between renders and triggers a re-render whenever it changes. The cart in the e-commerce page uses React Context precisely so multiple components (gallery, header, cart drawer) can all read and update the same cart state. You will finish the product page's cart interactivity today.

lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Tailwind CSS provides small, composable utility classes (`flex`, `gap-4`, `md:grid-cols-2`) applied directly in JSX, trading separate stylesheets for fast, consistent styling right where the markup lives. You will finish styling the full portfolio app's NavBar, ProjectCard grid, and ContactForm today.

lessons.title: Deploying to Vercel and final project
objectives: Deploy a real Next.js app to Vercel from a GitHub repo.
Do a final review pass across all three React projects from this module.
Present a finished, deployed full-stack web project as a portfolio piece.
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Learn

Vercel (made by the creators of Next.js) auto-detects a Next.js project and builds/deploys it with zero config — push to GitHub, import the repo, done. Today is final review and deployment: polish and ship the E-commerce Product Page, Social Media Feed Clone, and Full Portfolio React App, and confirm all three are live.
lessons.homework: Deploy your strongest of this module's three React projects (E-commerce Product Page, Social Media Feed Clone, Full Portfolio React App) to Vercel from GitHub. Do a final pass on all three, fix at least one real issue you find (a console warning, a broken prop, an unstyled element), and confirm the deployed link works in an incognito window.
